key_insight: Machine learning on wearable vaginal temperature data showed moderate ability to flag polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), suggesting temperature patterns may help screen for undiagnosed cases.
clinical_relevance: If validated, this approach could support earlier, lower-burden screening for PMOS using a consumer-accessible biosignal rather than relying only on clinic-based assessment.
method: 387 wearable-temperature monitor users completed a questionnaire and were filtered to those with enough cycle data and known PMOS status.
Three menstrual cycles per person were sampled and converted into cycle-level and user-level temperature features, including ovulation-related temperature rise metrics.
Models (Logistic Regression, SVM, Random Forest) were tested with 5-fold nested cross-validation at both cycle and user levels.
evidence_signal: In the abstract, the dataset included 387 participants with 49.6% self-reported PMOS, and model performance was described as moderate discrimination in cross-validated testing.
watch_item: Results are based on self-reported PMOS status and a selected subgroup with usable temperature data, so performance may not generalize to broader real-world screening.
paper_title: A digital health approach for identifying polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome using machine learning and body temperature
